records.name: Labuan
records.current_summary: Same-sex conduct is criminalised federally (penal-code provisions carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and caning), legal gender recognition is unavailable, and a dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only, while no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.  A 2022 Human Rights Watch report documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the federation. The audited sources document no Labuan-specific pattern; nationally applicable provisions govern here.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 16 Dec 2025): the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency' with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, while state Sharia enactments criminalise same-sex intimacy and 'cross-dressing' for Muslims only; no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded and discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement documented: since the 2018 election a crackdown has been underway — Oct 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and Nov 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Labuan.

Human Rights Watch / Justice for Sisters news release, 10 Aug 2022, on the report 'I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia': 73 LGBT people interviewed across Malaysia 2018-2021; documents the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021. The report's federal-territory Sharia-code finding is stated for Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya and is not extended to Labuan; no Labuan-specific enforcement case is documented.

records.name: Adygea
records.current_summary: The full federal framework applies: legal gender transition is banned, gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited, no discrimination protection exists, and the 'extremist movement' designation has produced 101 convictions by June 2025 (98 administrative, 3 criminal), with criminal cases pending against publishing-house staff facing up to 12 years.  A UK Home Office policy note judges North Caucasus residents, trans people and public activists likely to face persecution even where general LGB state-risk is not established; a foreign travel advisory likewise singles out the North Caucasus republics. The audited sources do not name Adygea within that exception, and no Adygea-specific evidence was documented, so national conditions with an unverified regional profile govern here.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025): assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Russia are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, but that people in the North Caucasus, trans people and those publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution — the record's own text confirms the note names Adygea in no such exception. It documents the national framework the record relies on: same-sex marriage and legal gender transition banned, trans-specific healthcare effectively banned since 2023, no discrimination protection, and 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Cloudflare block); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers general travel safety and, per the research dossier, the North Caucasus republics and interior-permission entry regimes.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions by June 2025 for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols — 98 administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges (two sentenced to prison, seventeen pending or unknown); on 15 May 2025 three staff of two publishing houses were charged with 'running an extremist organization' (article 282.2) and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable with up to four years in prison.

records.name: Buryatia
records.current_summary: The federal framework applies in full: transition and gender-affirming healthcare are banned, there is no discrimination protection, and the 'extremism' designation has produced 101 convictions since January 2024 (98 administrative, 3 criminal) while 'propaganda' penalties rose from 22 in 2021-2022 to 257 in 2023-2024, totalling over 63 million roubles in fines.  National support groups report emigration, asylum requests and the closure of queer spaces accelerating after the designation. The audited sources document no Buryatia-specific pattern, so national conditions govern what a visitor encounters here.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note on Russia (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) - the parent-framework document a visitor here stands under: same-sex activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison, and the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by 2-6 years and organising by 6-10 years. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and the note assesses trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. No region-specific findings: the document sets the national conditions in force across all of Russia, this region included.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (the site blocked automated access); the underlying foreign-government travel advisory for this country notes that official support is 'very limited' in parts of the country.

HRW report (30 June 2025): Russian courts issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions - approximately 98 administrative and three criminal - tied to the 'International Public LGBT Movement' designation; the Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation (two sentenced to prison; one died by suicide in pretrial detention), and 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, facing up to 12 years. No region-specific findings; documents the national enforcement climate governing visitors across all Russian regions.
